lessons.title: The development of understanding of genetics and evolution
lessons.summary: Trace how Darwin, Wallace and Mendel changed biology, weigh up the evidence from fossils, and see evolution happening today in antibiotic-resistant bacteria and the formation of new species.
objectives: I can describe Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection and explain why it was only gradually accepted.
I can compare Darwin's ideas with Lamarck's, and describe the contributions of Wallace and Mendel.
I can describe how fossils form, why the fossil record is incomplete, and how fossils provide evidence for evolution.
I can explain how new species form through isolation and natural selection, and give causes of extinction.
I can explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria evolve and describe how the spread of resistance can be reduced.

activities.title: Darwin's big idea
activities.content:
## Evolution by natural selection

In 1859 **Charles Darwin** published *On the Origin of Species*. After a five-year voyage around the world collecting specimens, years of experiments and discussion with other scientists, he proposed that all species evolved from simple life forms by **natural selection**:

1. Individuals in a species show a wide range of **variation** for a characteristic.
2. Organisms produce more offspring than can survive, so there is **competition** for food, mates and space.
3. Individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are **more likely to survive** and **breed**.
4. Those useful characteristics are **passed on** to the next generation.
5. Over many generations the characteristic becomes more common – the species has **evolved**.

A famous example is the Galápagos finches: on different islands Darwin found finches with beaks shaped for different foods – thick and strong for cracking seeds, thin and pointed for picking insects. He reasoned that they descended from one ancestral species that had spread to the islands and adapted to the food available on each.

Darwin's theory is now the accepted explanation for the diversity of life, but at the time it caused an uproar, and it took decades to be widely accepted.

activities.title: Lamarck, and why Darwin was doubted
activities.content:
## An earlier idea and a slow reception

Before Darwin, the French scientist **Jean-Baptiste Lamarck** suggested that changes an organism acquires **during its lifetime** are passed to its offspring. A giraffe stretching for high leaves would, he thought, grow a slightly longer neck and have longer-necked calves. We now know that acquired characteristics like this are **not inherited** – muscles you build or injuries you suffer do not change the genes in your sex cells. Lamarck's idea was wrong, but it shows that scientists were already discussing how species change.

**Why was Darwin's theory only gradually accepted?**

- It **challenged the belief** that God made all the animals and plants on Earth exactly as they are.
- There was **not enough evidence** at the time to convince many scientists.
- The **mechanism of inheritance** was unknown. Nobody could explain *how* characteristics were passed on, because genes and DNA were not discovered until much later.

Over the following decades, more fossils were found, the science of genetics developed, and Darwin's theory gained the evidence it had lacked. The story is a good example of how a scientific theory is judged: not on how clever it sounds, but on whether the evidence supports it.

question.text: Which of the following are reasons why Darwin's theory of evolution was only gradually accepted? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about beliefs at the time and about what scientists did not yet know.
question.explanation: The theory challenged religious beliefs about creation, there was little evidence at first, and the mechanism of inheritance was not understood. Darwin did publish his work, and it was not rejected because of his voyage.

options.text: It challenged the belief that God created all species
The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known
Darwin refused to publish his ideas
options.feedback: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

options.text: Darwin had never travelled to observe living things
options.feedback: Darwin spent five years collecting evidence on his voyage.

activities.title: Wallace and Mendel
activities.content:
## Two more pioneers

**Alfred Russel Wallace** worked at the same time as Darwin. Independently, he came up with the idea of natural selection, and in 1858 he and Darwin published their ideas jointly, which prompted Darwin to publish his book the following year. Wallace collected evidence around the world, especially in South-East Asia. He is best known for his work on **warning colouration** in animals – bright colours that tell predators an animal is poisonous or foul-tasting – and for his theory of **speciation**, which he developed further in the 1860s.

**Gregor Mendel** was a monk who, in the mid-19th century, carried out careful breeding experiments on **pea plants**. He tracked characteristics such as flower colour and seed shape over several generations and found that characteristics were passed on as **units** that did not blend. One "unit" (we now call it an **allele**) could be dominant over another. His work was published in 1866 but its importance was not recognised until after his death – scientists had no idea what the units were.

**How the understanding of genes developed**

| When | Discovery |
|---|---|
| 1866 | Mendel: inherited characteristics are determined by units (genes) |
| late 1800s | Chromosomes observed behaving in a way that matched Mendel's units during cell division |
| early 1900s | Scientists link Mendel's units to chromosomes; the word **gene** is introduced |
| 1953 | Structure of **DNA** worked out, explaining how genes are copied and passed on |

Once the mechanism of inheritance was understood, natural selection made much more sense – the missing piece in Darwin's theory had finally been found.

question.text: Put these discoveries in the order in which they happened.
question.hint: Mendel came first; the structure of DNA was the last piece of the puzzle.
question.explanation: Mendel's pea experiments (1860s) came first, then chromosomes were seen during cell division, then genes were linked to chromosomes, and finally the structure of DNA was determined in 1953.
order: Mendel shows characteristics are inherited as units
Chromosomes are observed during cell division
Genes are shown to be located on chromosomes
The structure of DNA is discovered

activities.title: Evidence from fossils
activities.content:
## What fossils tell us

A **fossil** is the remains or traces of an organism from millions of years ago, found in **rocks**. Fossils form in three main ways:

- **Parts that do not decay** – hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells survive when the conditions needed for decay (oxygen, moisture, warmth) are absent, e.g. deep in mud or ice.
- **Replacement by minerals** – as the organism decays slowly, minerals seep in and take its place, leaving a rock copy.
- **Preserved traces** – footprints, burrows, root channels and even droppings left in soft material that later hardened.

**Why is the fossil record incomplete?**

- Many early life forms were **soft-bodied**, so they decayed leaving no trace.
- Fossils only form under special conditions, so most organisms leave none.
- Many fossils that did form have been **destroyed** by geological activity such as earthquakes and volcanoes, or are buried too deep to find.

Because of these gaps, scientists cannot be certain how life on Earth began.

**How fossils support evolution**

By comparing fossils in rock layers of different ages, we can see how organisms have **changed gradually** over time – for example, the sequence of fossil horses shows the leg bones and teeth changing as grasslands spread. Fossils also show that many species that once lived are now **extinct**.

question.text: Why are there so few fossils of the earliest forms of life on Earth?
question.hint: Think about what those organisms were made of.
question.explanation: The earliest organisms were soft-bodied, so they decayed completely and left no fossils. Hard parts like shells and bones fossilise much more readily.

options.text: They were soft-bodied and decayed without leaving traces
They lived in places where rocks never form
They were too large to be buried
options.feedback: Early life forms were mostly tiny.

options.text: Scientists have not looked for them

activities.title: Extinction and speciation
activities.content:
## Species come and go

**Extinction** happens when there are **no remaining individuals** of a species alive. Causes include:

- new **predators**, **diseases** or **competitors** arriving (often introduced by humans);
- **changes to the environment** – the climate warming or cooling, habitats destroyed;
- a single **catastrophic event**, such as the asteroid impact linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs.

**Speciation – the formation of a new species**

A **species** is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce **fertile offspring**. New species form when populations of one species become so different that they can no longer do this. The process, as described by Darwin and Wallace, is:

1. **Isolation**: a population is split into two groups by a barrier such as a new river, a mountain range or a stretch of sea. The groups can no longer interbreed.
2. **Different conditions**: each group experiences a different environment with different food, predators or climate.
3. **Natural selection**: in each group, different characteristics are favoured, so the alleles that spread differ between the two populations.
4. **Different phenotypes**: over very many generations the two groups become **genetically and physically different**.
5. **New species**: if the groups are brought back together they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring – they are now two separate species.

In a six-mark speciation question, you must include *isolation*, *natural selection in each population* and *can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring*.

metadata.blanksText: Two populations of a species become separated by a barrier, which is called ___. Natural selection acts differently on each group, so their ___ become different. Eventually the two groups can no longer ___ to produce fertile offspring, so they are separate species.

question.hint: The first word means being cut off; the second is the observable characteristics; the third is what members of one species can do together.
question.explanation: Isolation splits the populations, natural selection produces different phenotypes, and the groups can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

activities.title: Antibiotic resistance: evolution in action
activities.content:
## Bacteria evolve fast

Bacteria reproduce by splitting in two, sometimes every 20 minutes, so a population can go through thousands of generations in a few weeks. That makes them ideal for watching natural selection happen.

**How a resistant strain develops**

1. Bacteria show variation because of random **mutations**. Occasionally a mutation makes a bacterium **resistant** to an antibiotic.
2. When the antibiotic is used, the non-resistant bacteria are **killed**, but the resistant ones **survive**.
3. With less competition, the resistant bacteria **reproduce rapidly**, and the resistance gene is passed to all their offspring.
4. The whole population becomes resistant. People infected with the resistant strain **cannot be treated** with that antibiotic.

**MRSA** is a well-known example: a strain of *Staphylococcus aureus* that is resistant to many antibiotics, including methicillin, and is a serious problem in hospitals where patients are already vulnerable.

**Slowing the spread of resistance**

- Doctors should **not prescribe antibiotics** inappropriately, e.g. for viral infections such as colds, which antibiotics cannot treat anyway.
- Patients must **complete the whole course**, so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and become resistant.
- **Restrict the use of antibiotics in farming**, where they are often given to healthy animals.

Developing new antibiotics is **costly and slow**, so it is unlikely to keep pace with new resistant strains. Prevention matters more than cure.

activities.title: Worked example: writing the resistance answer
activities.content:
**Question:** *A patient with a bacterial infection stops taking antibiotics after three days because they feel better. Explain how this could lead to a population of bacteria resistant to the antibiotic. (4 marks)*

**Model answer, one idea per line:**

1. Not all the bacteria were killed – the ones still alive after three days are likely to be those with a **mutation** giving some **resistance**.
2. With the antibiotic gone, and the non-resistant bacteria dead, the resistant bacteria face **less competition**.
3. They **reproduce rapidly** and pass on the resistance **gene/allele** to their offspring.
4. The resistance allele becomes **more common**, so the population is now **resistant** and the antibiotic will not work on it.

**What examiners want to see**

- The word **mutation** as the source of the variation (never say bacteria "learn" or "become immune" – immunity is what *our* bodies develop).
- A clear statement that the resistant bacteria **survive and reproduce** while others die.
- The idea that the characteristic is **inherited** by offspring.

This is just natural selection applied to bacteria, so if you can write a Darwin answer, you can write this one.

question.text: Describe three ways in which the development of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria can be slowed down.
question.hint: Think about doctors, patients and farmers.
question.explanation: Doctors should avoid prescribing antibiotics for non-serious or viral infections; patients should finish their full course so that no bacteria survive; and the use of antibiotics in farming should be restricted.

markScheme.criterion: Doctors should not overprescribe / not prescribe for viral infections
Patients should complete the full course of antibiotics
Restrict the use of antibiotics in agriculture / farming

question.text:
A population of lizards lived on one large island. Rising sea levels split the island into two smaller islands. Thousands of years later, the lizards on the two islands look different, and when brought together they cannot produce fertile offspring.

Explain how the two populations of lizards have become separate species. **(5 marks)**
question.hint: Structure your answer: isolation → different conditions → natural selection in each population → different characteristics → can no longer interbreed.
question.explanation: The rising sea isolated the two populations so they could not interbreed. The two islands had different conditions, such as different food or predators. In each population, individuals with the characteristics best suited to their island survived and reproduced, passing on their alleles (natural selection). Over many generations, the phenotypes and alleles of the two groups became increasingly different. Eventually they were so different that they could not interbreed to produce fertile offspring, which is the definition of separate species.

markScheme.criterion: The populations were geographically isolated so could not interbreed
The two islands had different environmental conditions / selection pressures
Natural selection: individuals with favourable variation survive and reproduce
Advantageous alleles / characteristics are passed on so the populations become genetically different over many generations
Eventually cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring so are separate species

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Darwin**: evolution by **natural selection** – variation, competition, survival of the best adapted, characteristics passed on.
- Slow to be accepted because it **challenged religious beliefs**, lacked **evidence** and the **mechanism of inheritance** was unknown. **Lamarck** wrongly thought acquired characteristics were inherited.
- **Wallace** independently proposed natural selection and worked on warning colouration and speciation. **Mendel's** pea experiments showed inheritance in units – later linked to chromosomes, genes and DNA (1953).
- **Fossils** form from hard parts, mineral replacement or traces; the record is incomplete (soft bodies decay, special conditions needed, fossils destroyed).
- **Extinction**: new predators, disease, competitors, environmental change, catastrophes.
- **Speciation**: isolation → different conditions → natural selection → different phenotypes → can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
- **Antibiotic resistance** evolves by mutation and natural selection (e.g. **MRSA**). Reduce it by not overprescribing, completing courses and restricting farm use.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Lamarck believed that characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime could be passed on to its offspring.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Lamarck proposed that acquired characteristics are inherited. This idea has since been shown to be wrong.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which scientist carried out breeding experiments on pea plants that revealed how characteristics are inherited?
practiceQuestions.hint: He was a monk whose work was only appreciated after his death.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gregor Mendel studied pea plants and showed that characteristics are inherited as separate units, which we now call genes.

options.text: Gregor Mendel
Charles Darwin
Alfred Russel Wallace
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck

practiceQuestions.text: Alfred Russel Wallace is best known for his work on which of the following?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about brightly coloured, poisonous animals.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Wallace studied warning colouration in animals and developed the theory of speciation, as well as independently proposing natural selection.

options.text: Warning colouration in animals
The structure of DNA
options.feedback: DNA's structure was discovered in 1953, long after Wallace.

options.text: Blood glucose control
Photosynthesis in leaves

practiceQuestions.text: Match each way a fossil can form to the correct example.
practiceQuestions.hint: Footprints are traces; shells are hard parts; a rock copy is replacement.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A dinosaur footprint is a preserved trace; a shell that survives in mud is a part that does not decay; a stone copy of a bone forms by mineral replacement.

pairs.right: A dinosaur footprint hardened in mud
A shell buried where there is no oxygen
A bone gradually turned to stone

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following can cause a species to become extinct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Anything that stops every individual from surviving or breeding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A new predator and a catastrophic event such as an asteroid impact can both wipe out a species. Producing many offspring and having lots of variation both make extinction less likely, not more.

options.text: A new predator arriving in the habitat
A catastrophic event such as an asteroid impact
Producing a large number of offspring
Having a lot of genetic variation
options.feedback: Variation helps a species adapt to change.

metadata.blanksText: A species is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce ___ offspring. The formation of a new species is called ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: The offspring must be able to reproduce themselves.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Members of a species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; speciation is the formation of a new species.

practiceQuestions.text: A single bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, how many bacteria will there be after 2 hours?
practiceQuestions.hint: Work out how many divisions happen in 2 hours, then double the population that many times.

practiceQuestions.text: Put the stages in the correct order to describe how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
practiceQuestions.hint: It starts with a random change in the DNA.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A mutation gives resistance; the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria; the resistant ones survive and reproduce; the resistance gene spreads through the population.
order: A random mutation makes one bacterium resistant
The antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria
The resistant bacterium survives and reproduces
The resistance gene is passed to the offspring

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why scientists cannot be certain about how life on Earth began.
practiceQuestions.hint: What evidence would they need, and why is it missing?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The fossil record is incomplete. The earliest organisms were soft-bodied so left few fossils, fossils only form in special conditions, and many have been destroyed by geological activity.

markScheme.criterion: The fossil record is incomplete / few early fossils exist
Reason: early organisms soft-bodied / decayed, or fossils destroyed by geological activity

practiceQuestions.text:
MRSA is a strain of bacteria that is resistant to several antibiotics.

(a) Explain why MRSA is a particular problem in hospitals. **(1 mark)**

(b) Explain why it is difficult to solve the problem of antibiotic resistance simply by developing new antibiotics. **(3 marks)**
practiceQuestions.hint: For (b) think about cost, time and how quickly bacteria evolve.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Hospitals contain many vulnerable patients with wounds or weak immune systems, and the bacteria spread easily between them. (b) Developing new antibiotics is very expensive and takes many years, whereas bacteria reproduce rapidly and new resistant strains can appear quickly, so development cannot keep up.

markScheme.criterion: Patients are vulnerable / infection spreads easily between patients
Development is slow / takes many years
Bacteria reproduce quickly so new resistant strains appear faster than new antibiotics

practiceQuestions.text: Describe how Darwin's theory of natural selection would explain why giraffes have long necks, and state how this differs from Lamarck's explanation.
practiceQuestions.hint: Darwin starts with variation that already exists; Lamarck starts with an individual changing during its life.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Darwin: giraffes naturally varied in neck length; those with longer necks could reach more leaves, so they were more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on the alleles for long necks, which became more common over generations. Lamarck: each giraffe stretched its neck during its life and passed the longer neck to its offspring – an acquired characteristic, which we now know cannot be inherited.

markScheme.criterion: Variation in neck length existed; longer-necked giraffes could reach more food and were more likely to survive
They reproduced and passed on the alleles/characteristic, so it became more common
Lamarck: neck lengthened by stretching during life and this acquired change was passed on
